name: Vaal-Orange
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Wuras, C. F. 1919/20. An Outline of the Bushman Language [ed. Bourquin], grammar sketch (Bantu Studies); not found online

sources.citation: Bleek, Dorothea F. 1956. A Bushman Dictionary (American Oriental Series 41). New Haven: American Oriental Society. Introduction (classification: SIIc ǁkuǁe near Theunissen, D. Bleek's own data; SIId Seroa near Bethany, Wuras & Arbousset) and letter-section notes.
sources.note: No Vaal-Orange-specific stress statement. Only a family-wide aside under 'n & ŋ': 'In pure Bushman languages these nasals do not often occur as initial sounds, but are frequently found in unstressed second syllables and at the end of words.' Also notes 'variations in tone' under a.

sources.citation: Wuras, C. F. (ed. Walther Bourquin). 1919/20. An Outline of the Bushman Language. Zeitschrift für Eingeborenen-Sprachen 10: 81-87. (Glottolog's only descriptive ref; earlier scan mis-cited it as Bantu Studies.) Found inside the Toronto scan 'Afrika und Übersee... v.09-10' = Zeitschrift für Kolonialsprachen/ZfES IX-X on archive.org.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Read in full (pp. 81-87). Nothing on word stress/accent. Only sound remarks: 'The words of this language are mostly monosyllables' (p.81), click descriptions, and p.86 'Some words are exactly alike... and are spoken in a lower and higher key to distinguish them' (i.e. tone). Dialect described: 'that of the bushmen who lived formerly on Riet & Kaffir river' (ǁKuǁe/Bethany, OFS).

sources.citation: Arbousset, Thomas & François Daumas. 1842. Relation d'un voyage d'exploration au nord-est de la colonie du Cap de Bonne-Espérance. Paris: Arthus Bertrand. Remarks on the Séroa (Baroa) language pp. 506-509; 'Vocabulaire séroa' pp. 509ff. (primary source for the Seroa dialect, D. Bleek's SIId).
sources.note: No word-stress statement. p.508: 'Au contraire, les accents le sont beaucoup [variés], et le sens d'un même mot tout à fait différent, suivant la manière de le prononcer. Ainsi, N'go signifie un dieu; kho, de l'eau; khô, un blanc... Cela rappelle ce qu'on dit à ce sujet du chinois' -- a pre-scientific remark on tone-like distinctions, not stress placement.

sources.citation: Güldemann, Tom. 2019. Toward a subclassification of the ǃUi branch of Tuu (ms., 10 pp.); Güldemann, Tom. 2014. 'Khoisan' linguistic classification today. In Güldemann & Fehn (eds.), Beyond 'Khoisan', 1-43. Amsterdam: Benjamins.
